name: Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration
aliases: neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation type 1

reference.source: Movement-disorder and neurogenetics textbooks with peer-reviewed reviews
clinicalPearls: Most common form of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA), inherited autosomal recessively through biallelic PANK2 variants
Classic early-onset form presents in childhood with gait disturbance, dystonia, rigidity, and pigmentary retinopathy, progressing over years
Atypical later-onset form has slower progression with prominent speech and neuropsychiatric features and less retinopathy
Oromandibular and limb dystonia can be severe and may lead to status dystonicus, a neurological emergency

The pathognomonic MRI finding is the eye-of-the-tiger sign: a central region of T2 hyperintensity within surrounding hypointensity in the globus pallidus, reflecting focal gliosis amid iron deposition
Iron-sensitive MRI sequences (T2*/gradient-echo/susceptibility-weighted imaging) accentuate the pallidal iron and support the NBIA diagnosis
Management is symptomatic, targeting dystonia and spasticity with oral agents, botulinum toxin, and in selected refractory cases deep brain stimulation
Diagnosis is confirmed by PANK2 molecular testing in the setting of the characteristic clinical and imaging picture
reference.pathophysiology: Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in PANK2, encoding a mitochondrial pantothenate kinase that catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of coenzyme A biosynthesis from vitamin B5. Impaired coenzyme A synthesis is thought to disrupt lipid and energy metabolism and to allow accumulation of cysteine-containing substrates that chelate iron, driving oxidative damage. The net effect is progressive iron deposition and neurodegeneration concentrated in the globus pallidus, producing the extrapyramidal features and the characteristic pallidal imaging changes.
additionalDifferentials: Other NBIA subtypes (PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration, BPAN, aceruloplasminaemia, neuroferritinopathy)
Dopa-responsive dystonia and other early-onset dystonias
Mitochondrial disorders with basal ganglia involvement
Secondary pallidal injury from hypoxia or manganese exposure
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI including iron-sensitive sequences to demonstrate the eye-of-the-tiger sign and pallidal iron
PANK2 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Ophthalmological assessment including electroretinography for pigmentary retinopathy
Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease
Serum ferritin and caeruloplasmin to help distinguish other NBIA subtypes
redFlags: Status dystonicus with unremitting severe dystonia causing pain, hyperthermia, or rhabdomyolysis
Acute swallowing failure with aspiration risk
Rapid loss of ambulation or new bulbar dysfunction
reference.prognosis: The classic childhood-onset form is progressive, with most patients losing independent ambulation within years of onset, whereas the atypical form advances more slowly over decades. Life expectancy is reduced, largely from complications of severe dystonia and immobility.
pitfalls: Mistaking the eye-of-the-tiger appearance for another basal ganglia lesion or dismissing subtle pallidal iron on standard sequences
Failing to obtain iron-sensitive MRI sequences that reveal the diagnostic iron deposition
Overlooking status dystonicus as an emergency requiring prompt escalation
Not screening for Wilson disease, a treatable mimic, before settling on an NBIA diagnosis
